title: Altair Aether
note: Our own design: a ~300 kg lunar communications relay, fired off a mass driver near the lunar south pole into an elliptical frozen lunar orbit, built from real flight hardware where it exists. Frame: x along the track (the direction of travel, and the craft's axis: the launch load runs down it), z up, y left. The craft's separation plane is at x = 0; the sled and the rails are behind and below it. Pass 1: structure, tank, main thruster, sled and rails. Pass 2: propulsion (eight 1 N thrusters, latch valve, fill and drain valves, lines). Pass 3: power (two solar wings, deployed; two batteries). Pass 4: comms (S-band dish to the Moon on +z, X-band array to the Earth on +x, transponder). Pass 5: attitude (four reaction wheels, two star trackers, sun sensors, IMU). Pass 6: electronics (power control unit, power cables; a reserved slot for the flight computer and valve drivers, which are designed separately). Pass 7: thermal (silvered-Teflon radiators on five sides, a blanket on the Moon-facing top, heaters). Pass 8: deployment (wings folded on hinges for the launch, hold-downs; click a wing to unfold).

open_questions: Launch geometry (decided 2026-11-03: a flat shot): a flat 2.18 km/s shot from the south-pole site puts the orbit's high point over the north pole, so the craft first serves the north. Serving the south pole needs the high point turned round (argument of periselene, a large burn the 550 m/s budget only partly covers), a launch site near the north pole, or the relay accepted over the north.
Lunar Pathfinder's orbit differs between SSTL's guide (673 x 7331 km, 54.9°) and a 2022 NASA slide (500 x 7500 km, 57.8°); SSTL calls its values indicative.
A south-pole launch site reaches inclinations near 90° directly; the 54.9° orbit needs a site at or below about 55°S, or a plane change.
Propulsion has no filter or pressure transducer yet (no sourced part found); the thruster layout is our own, not copied from a flown craft.

Comms: no low-gain S-band antenna yet for safe mode (no maker's datasheet found); the EnduroSat array's band (8025-8400 MHz) sits below the 8450-8500 MHz lunar band; with the dish on the Moon and the array on the Earth, the wings turning only about y lose some sunlight in some seasons.
Attitude: the wheel pyramid's tilt and the sensors' places are our own; coverage of the two coarse sun sensors is not a full sphere (safe mode would also lean on the fine sensor and the trackers).

Electronics: the Starbuck-Mini is rated 20 kRAD and '5–7 years in LEO'; whether that covers five years in lunar orbit (no Van Allen belts to cross, since it launches from the Moon, but solar particle events) isn't checked. Its bus follows the battery (22-34 V), not a regulated 28 V. The flight computer and valve drivers come from the separate design; the power budget waits for them.

Thermal: sized by hand for the worst cold-side case (600 W, no sun); not checked against the hot case at periselene (the sunlit Moon's infrared on the radiators) or the 2 h shadow (heater power). Lines and valves need heaters too (not modelled).

Deployment: the wings are shown folded for the launch (click a wing to unfold it); the hold-downs are placeholders, the dish's launch lock and the panels' hinge hardware aren't modelled, and the wing drive's size is still an estimate.
